power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Conceptualisation, Writing-review and editing.
Born in Bradford is only possible because of the enthusiasm and commitment of the children and parents in Born in Bradford.
We are grateful to all the participants, health professionals, schools and researchers who have made Born in Bradford happen.
We would also like to thank the entire Born in Bradford data team for their support.
A substantial body of research has established associations between parental emotional difficulties and children's social-emotional functioning.

For example, a meta-analysis of about 200,000 mother-child dyads reported associations between maternal perinatal anxiety and depression and child socialemotional difficulties across childhood through to adolescence (Rogers et al., 2020).
text.formatted: For example, a meta-analysis of about 200,000 mother-child dyads reported associations between maternal perinatal anxiety and depression and child socialemotional difficulties across childhood through to adolescence <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Rogers et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond the perinatal period, studies have shown significant associations between parental (both mothers and fathers) anxiety and depression and child emotional and behavioural difficulties such as internalising and externalising problems (Goodman et al., 2011; Ivanova et al., 2022; Rogers et al., 2020; Sweeney & Wilson, 2023).
text.formatted: Beyond the perinatal period, studies have shown significant associations between parental (both mothers and fathers) anxiety and depression and child emotional and behavioural difficulties such as internalising and externalising problems <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Goodman et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Ivanova et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Rogers et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Sweeney & Wilson, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: A more recent meta-analysis also found that clinical levels of parental depression is a significant risk factor for child emotional difficulties (Aaron et al., 2024).
text.formatted: A more recent meta-analysis also found that clinical levels of parental depression is a significant risk factor for child emotional difficulties <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Aaron et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: While these findings highlight the link between parent and child emotional wellbeing, much of this work focuses on how parent's difficulties affect children.
Developmental theories and recent approaches provide a useful way into this.

For example, the transactional model describes development as process in which children and caregivers continually shape one another's experiences though everyday interactions (Sameroff, 2009) Theories of evocative child effects and empirical studies of reciprocal parent-child processes make a similar point: children actively help to shape their caregiving environments rather than simply responding to them (Avinun & Knafo, 2014; Scarr & McCartney, 1983).
text.formatted: For example, the transactional model describes development as process in which children and caregivers continually shape one another's experiences though everyday interactions (Sameroff, 2009) Theories of evocative child effects and empirical studies of reciprocal parent-child processes make a similar point: children actively help to shape their caregiving environments rather than simply responding to them <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Avinun & Knafo, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Scarr & McCartney, 1983)</ref>.

text.text: Longitudinal findings fit with this, with children's conduct problems predicting subsequent changes in parenting practices (Pardini et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Longitudinal findings fit with this, with children's conduct problems predicting subsequent changes in parenting practices <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Pardini et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: As Wade and colleagues (2026) recently pointed out, the overwhelming emphasis on parent-tochild effects in the literature risks overlooking the reciprocal interactions through which parents and children shape one another's experiences.
text.formatted: As <ref type="bibr">Wade and colleagues (2026)</ref> recently pointed out, the overwhelming emphasis on parent-tochild effects in the literature risks overlooking the reciprocal interactions through which parents and children shape one another's experiences.

text.text: Parenting is particularly important to this broader understanding of family emotional system as it provides an everyday context in which parent and child experiences come together.

Parents bring their own emotional experiences to interactions with their children, while children's emotional, behavioural, and temperamental characteristics may elicit different responses from their caregivers.

Consistent with this, a recent systematic review and meta-analysis found that parental anxiety and depression were associated with greater parenting stress less effective parental discipline, and lower parenting self-efficacy and affection (Bennett et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Consistent with this, a recent systematic review and meta-analysis found that parental anxiety and depression were associated with greater parenting stress less effective parental discipline, and lower parenting self-efficacy and affection <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bennett et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, parenting does not occur independently of the child.
As such, another meta-analytic evidence indicates that children's externalising difficulties predict subsequent changes in parenting (Pinquart, 2017).
text.formatted: As such, another meta-analytic evidence indicates that children's externalising difficulties predict subsequent changes in parenting <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Pinquart, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Parenting characteristics may therefore reflect both parents' emotional experiences and their responses to the needs and behaviours of their children.

Some studies also point towards reciprocal associations between children's behavioural difficulties and parenting, whereby child behaviour predicts subsequent changes in parenting as well as parenting predicting subsequent changes in child behaviour (Pardini et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Some studies also point towards reciprocal associations between children's behavioural difficulties and parenting, whereby child behaviour predicts subsequent changes in parenting as well as parenting predicting subsequent changes in child behaviour <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Pardini et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Parenting may therefore represent an important relational interface between maternal and child functioning: it is associated with parents' own psychological wellbeing while also occurring within an interpersonal context that children actively help to shape.

Accordingly, understanding parental emotional difficulties and children's social-emotional functioning may require moving beyond models in which parenting is positioned solely as a mechanism transmitting parental risk to children, towards a framework in which maternal functioning, parenting, and child functioning are considered jointly as interconnected components of the family system.
A further consideration is that associations between broad measures may conceal differences between specific experiences.
Anxiety and depression encompass symptoms that may relate differently to parenting or child functioning.
Similarly, children's emotional symptoms, conduct difficulties, hyperactivity, peer problems, and prosocial behaviour capture distinct aspects of their social-emotional functioning.

Network approaches provide a way to examine these experiences in a greater detail (e.g., symptom level) while considering their connections within broader experiences (e.g., parent and child emotions).
Network theory proposes that psychological difficulties can develop and persist through interactions among symptoms (Borsboom, 2017).
text.formatted: Network theory proposes that psychological difficulties can develop and persist through interactions among symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Borsboom, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Drawing on this proposition, we can examine the complex interactions between specific parental emotional symptoms and child's social-emotional functioning within a broader family emotional system.

More specifically, it can help us identify which parental and child factors are most influential on the wider family emotional system and which factors (e.g., parenting) may play a role to connect parent-child emotional and behavioural difficulties.

This could help generate hypotheses about where interventions may have the greatest impact across family emotional systems, that is, where improvements in one area may support positive change in others, instead of targeting parent or child outcomes in isolation.
Despite extensive evidence linking maternal psychological distress with children's social-emotional functioning, three important gaps remain.

First, the literature continues to be dominated by parent-tochild explanations, despite developmental theory and emerging evidence suggesting that children actively participate in shaping family interactions.

Second, reliance on aggregate measures of maternal psychopathology has provided limited insight into whether individual maternal symptoms occupy different positions in relation to parenting and distinct domains of child functioning.

At the same time, treating child social-emotional functioning as a single overall construct may obscure potentially important differences between emotional, behavioural, attentional, peer, and prosocial domains.
The current study examines maternal depressive and anxiety symptoms, parenting characteristics, and distinct domains of children's social-emotional functioning as an interconnected system.
Using network analysis, we explore the overall structure connecting these experiences and whether they form distinct but connected communities.
We also examine which maternal symptoms, parenting characteristics, and child domains are most strongly connected within the overall network, and which factors act as bridges across communities.

Together, these questions allow us to consider maternal and child functioning jointly and generate hypotheses about where coordinated support may benefit parents and children within their shared family system.
We made use of secondary data from Born in Bradford (BiB); a population-based birth cohort study in Bradford, United Kingdom.
The BiB cohort recruited 12,453 women across 13,776 pregnancies between 2007 and 2011.
We used data from the BiB Growing Up cohort, which was a follow-up study when children were of primary-school age.
Further details of BiB cohort and the Growing Up followup are reported elsewhere (Bird et al., 2019; McEachan et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Further details of BiB cohort and the Growing Up followup are reported elsewhere <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bird et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">McEachan et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In the BiB Growing Up cohort, there were 5,318 mothers and 9,805 children.

For the current study, we created mother-child dyads of 5,143 participants (i.e., mother + child dyad with information in at least one focal variable) with children being at approximate 9 years of age (SD=1.02) and mothers being approximately 38 years old.
Of these, the majority of mothers were from Pakistani background (55.6), followed by White (31.4%), Indian (3.6%), Bangladeshi (3.1%), other ethnic backgrounds (6%).
Ethnicity information was missing for a small sample (0.3%).
Child social-emotional functioning was measured using the parent-reported Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ; Goodman, 1997).
text.formatted: Child social-emotional functioning was measured using the parent-reported Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ; <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Goodman, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: The SDQ is a 25-item measure answered on a three-point Likert-type scale (0=Not true,1= Somewhat true, 2-Certainly true) with five subscales: emotional symptoms, conduct problems, hyperactivity/inattention, peer relationship problems, and prosocial behaviour.
We entered total scores for each of the five subscales as a node, rather than entering individual SDQ items into the network model.
This allowed child functioning to be modelled at the level of theoretically and clinically interpretable social-emotional domains.
Additionally, we reversescored emotional symptoms, conduct problems, hyperactivity and inattention, and peer problems, so that higher scores represented better functioning and fewer difficulties.
Mothers reported their anxiety symptoms on the standardised Generalized Anxiety Disorder scale (GAD-7; Spitzer et al., 2006).
text.formatted: Mothers reported their anxiety symptoms on the standardised Generalized Anxiety Disorder scale <ref type="bibr">(GAD-7;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Spitzer et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: The GAD-7 is a 4-point Likert-type scale (responses ranging from0=not at all to3=nearly everyday) measuring the following anxiety symptoms over the past two weeks: 1-nervousness, 2-inability to control worrying, 3-excessive worry, 4-difficulty relaxing, 5restlessness, 6-irritability, and 7-fear that something awful might happen.
Each item was reversescored and individually entered into the network model with higher scores indicating lower anxiety symptoms.
Maternal depression symptoms were assessed using the eight-item Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-8, Kroenke et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Maternal depression symptoms were assessed using the eight-item Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-8, <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Kroenke et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: The measure asks about the following symptoms experienced in the past two weeks: diminished interest or pleasure, depressed mood, sleep disturbance, fatigue or low energy, appetite disturbance, negative self-evaluation, concentration difficulties, and psychomotor slowing or agitation.
Both anxiety and depression scales were answered on a 4-point Likert-type scale ranging from experiencing them from not at all (0) to nearly every day (3).
Each symptom was entered as a separate node so that higher scores represented lower depression symptoms.
Parenting was assessed using parent-reported items drawn from Growing Up in Australia, the Longitudinal Study of Australian Children (Bird et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Parenting was assessed using parent-reported items drawn from Growing Up in Australia, the Longitudinal Study of Australian Children <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bird et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Three distinct parenting domains were measured in the cohort: perceived parental efficacy, parental affection, and strict parenting.
To note, parenting measures were only available for a smaller proportion of the sample (n = 358), the implications of which are explicitly evaluated in limitations section.
Mothers rated their own perceived parental competence in regard to caring for and responding to their child on a 10-point scale (responses ranging from1=not at all how I feel to1=exactly how I feel).

The scale consisted of four questions: "I feel I am very good at keeping this child amused", "I feel that I am very good at calming this child when he/she is upset", "I feel I am very good at keeping this child busy while I am doing housework", and "I feel I am very good at routine tasks of caring for child feeding".
These items were summed to generate a parental efficacy variable with higher scores representing greater parenting efficacy.
Mothers reported how often they expressed affection and closeness with their child on a 5-point Likert-type scale (ranging from never/almost never to always/almost always).

The scale consisted of six items: "How often do you express affection by hugging, kissing and holding this child?", "How often do you hug or hold this child for no particular reason?", "How often do you tell this child how happy he/she makes you?", "How often do you have warm, close times together with this child?", "How often do you enjoy doing things with this child?", and "How often do you feel close to your child when they are happy or upset?".
We summed these items to generate an overall maternal affection score, with higher values representing greater, affectionate parenting.
Mothers rated their strict parenting practices on a 10-point scale ranging from (1=not at all to10=all the time).

The scale consisted of five items: "I have been angry with this child", "I have raised my voice with or shouted at this child", "When this child cries, he/she gets on my nerves", "I have lost my temper with this child", and "I have left my child alone in their bedroom when they were upset".
A summed score was calculated and reverse-scored so that higher scores represented less strict parenting.
All analyses were conducted in R (R Core Team, 2026).
Descriptive statistics (frequencies, means, and standard deviations) were reported to outline the sample characteristics.
We used the bootnet, qgraph, igraph, and networktools packages.
Specifically, we estimated a regularised Gaussian Graphical Model (GGM) consisting of 23 nodes.

The network was estimated from Pearson correlations using the graphical least absolute shrinkage and selection operator, with model selection based on the Extended Bayesian Information Criterion (EBICglasso; γ = .50), implemented in the bootnet package.
Missing data were handled using pairwise deletion, with each correlation estimated from dyads with observed information on both variables.
Hence, the number of observations contributing to each association potentially varied.
Additionally, we used LASSO regularisation which shrinks small associations towards zero, producing a sparse network in which retained edges represent regularised partial correlations.
In this network, blue edges indicate positive conditional associations in the expected direction while red edges indicate negative conditional associations.
We used cross-sectional data, hence, all edges represent undirected conditional relationships.
We took a data-driven community detection approach to explore the organisation of nodes in the network.
We used the Walktrap algorithm, implemented in igraph package.
As Walktrap does not support negative edges, these were set to zero for community detection.
We expected maternal depression, maternal anxiety, parenting, and child social-emotional functioning forming separate communities corresponding to their theoretical measurement domains.
We used these community memberships in reporting bridge centrality and bridge centrality bootstraps.

We reported the positions and connectivity of individuals nodes within the overall network using three global centrality measures: strength, expected influence, and betweenness using the qgraph package.

Strength quantifies the sum of the absolute edge weights connecting a node to the remainder of the network; expected influence retains the signs of those associations and is therefore informative in networks containing both positive and negative edges; and Betweenness outlines the frequency with which a node lies along shortest paths connecting other nodes (Epskamp & Fried, 2018).
text.formatted: Strength quantifies the sum of the absolute edge weights connecting a node to the remainder of the network; expected influence retains the signs of those associations and is therefore informative in networks containing both positive and negative edges; and Betweenness outlines the frequency with which a node lies along shortest paths connecting other nodes <ref type="bibr">(Epskamp & Fried, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: We also examined how different communities connect to one another using bridge centrality measures in the networktools package.
Bridge strength and one-step bridge expected influence were used to identify nodes with comparatively strong connections to nodes outside their own empirically detected community.
Finally, bridge betweenness was reported to show how often a node lies on the shortest paths between nodes belonging different communities.
We tested the stability and the accuracy of the reported network using bootstrap procedures in the bootnet package.
In regard to network accuracy, edge-weight accuracy was tested using 1,000 nonparametric bootstrap samples, generating bootstrap confidence intervals around estimated edge weights.
We also used bootstrap difference tests to assess the statistical differences in strength between different edges.
In terms of stability estimations, stability of centrality estimates was evaluated using case-dropping bootstrap analysis with 1,000 bootstrap samples.

Correlation-stability coefficients were calculated to quantify the proportion of observations that could be dropped while retaining a correlation of at least .70 (with 95% probability) between samples.
As suggested (Epskamp et al., 2018), CS coefficients above .25 were considered acceptable.
text.formatted: As suggested <ref type="bibr">(Epskamp et al., 2018)</ref>, CS coefficients above .25 were considered acceptable.

text.text: Before examining the network structure, we assessed pairwise correlations among the included variables, which were predominantly positive, reflecting that all nodes were coded on the same direction with higher scores indicating better functioning (Figure S1).
text.formatted: Before examining the network structure, we assessed pairwise correlations among the included variables, which were predominantly positive, reflecting that all nodes were coded on the same direction with higher scores indicating better functioning (Figure <ref type="figure">S1</ref>).

text.text: The EBICglasso-regularised network revealed a structured pattern of conditional associations across maternal anxiety and depression, parenting characteristics, and child social-emotional functioning (Figure 1).
text.formatted: The EBICglasso-regularised network revealed a structured pattern of conditional associations across maternal anxiety and depression, parenting characteristics, and child social-emotional functioning (Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: The strongest and densest connections were generally observed among nodes belonging to the same theoretical construct (e.g., maternal anxiety), alongside a smaller number of cross-domain associations.

For mothers, the strongest connection was between inability to control worrying and excessive worry (GAD2-GAD3; r = .51), followed by anhedonia and depressed mood (PHQ1-PHQ2; .33), sleep difficulties and little energy (PHQ-3-PHQ-4; .29), and difficulty relaxing and restlessness (GAD4-GAD5; .29).
For children, the strongest connection appeared to be between conduct problems and hyperactivity/inattention (.31).
The data-driven community detection closely reflected the theoretical organisation of the measures.

Maternal depressive and anxiety symptoms formed separate communities, while emotional symptoms, conduct problems, hyperactivity/inattention, peer problems, and prosocial behaviour clustered together as a distinct child-functioning community.
Maternal efficacy, maternal affection, and strict parenting similarly formed a coherent parenting community, visually placed in between maternal and child outcomes.

Connection between this community and the maternal emotional symptoms and child social-emotional functioning were examined using bridge centrality metrics, while the overall influence of the nodes were evaluated using global centrality metrics reported below.
We examined strength, expected influence, and betweenness to identify prominent nodes in the overall network (Figure 2).
text.formatted: We examined strength, expected influence, and betweenness to identify prominent nodes in the overall network (Figure <ref type="figure">2</ref>).

text.text: Maternal anxiety symptoms were the most central nodes.
Difficulty relaxing (GAD-4; strength = 1.26) showed the highest strength, followed by excessive worry (GAD-3; 1.24) and inability to control worrying (GAD-2; 1.24).
Conduct problems were the most central child domain (1.20) and ranked fourth overall.
Expected influence showed a similar pattern, indicating that network connectivity was concentrated around maternal worry-related anxiety symptoms and child conduct problems.
Betweenness differed, with strict parenting (63) and conduct problems (49) occupying the most prominent intermediary positions.
We examined bridge strength, bridge expected influence, and bridge betweenness to identify nodes connecting different network communities (Figure 3).
text.formatted: We examined bridge strength, bridge expected influence, and bridge betweenness to identify nodes connecting different network communities (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">3</ref>).

text.text: Parenting nodes showed the highest bridge strength, led by strict parenting (0.90), maternal affection (0.74), and maternal efficacy (0.66).
In contrast, maternal irritability (GAD-6) showed the highest bridge expected influence (0.51), followed by difficulty relaxing (GAD-4; 0.46) and negative self-evaluation (PHQ-6; 0.43).
Strict parenting also showed the highest bridge betweenness (57), followed by maternal efficacy (48) and conduct problems (43).
Overall, parenting characteristics were prominent cross-community connectors, while maternal irritability showing the strongest connections to the nodes outside its own community.
Global centrality estimates for the mother-child network Bridge centrality estimates for the mother-child network
Bootstrap confidence intervals varied considerably in width, indicating greater uncertainty around some edge-weight estimates than others (Figure S2).
text.formatted: Bootstrap confidence intervals varied considerably in width, indicating greater uncertainty around some edge-weight estimates than others (Figure <ref type="figure">S2</ref>).

text.text: Several confidence intervals include zero, hence, caution needs to be taken when interpreting certain individual associations.

Bootstrap difference tests indicated that some of the strongest edges differed significantly from the weaker edges, although differences between similarly sized edges could not always be reliably distinguished (Figure S3).
text.formatted: Bootstrap difference tests indicated that some of the strongest edges differed significantly from the weaker edges, although differences between similarly sized edges could not always be reliably distinguished (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">S3</ref>).

text.text: Likewise, the node strength difference test did not clearly distinguish all the highest-ranked nodes from one another (Figure S4).
text.formatted: Likewise, the node strength difference test did not clearly distinguish all the highest-ranked nodes from one another (Figure <ref type="figure">S4</ref>).

text.text: Hence, centrality metrics should be interpreted within these limitations.

In terms of the stability of the global centrality measures, case-dropping analyses indicated excellent stability for expected influence (CS = .75), acceptable stability for strength (CS = .44), but poor stability for betweenness (CS = .13; Figure S5).
text.formatted: In terms of the stability of the global centrality measures, case-dropping analyses indicated excellent stability for expected influence (CS = .75), acceptable stability for strength (CS = .44), but poor stability for betweenness (CS = .13; Figure <ref type="figure">S5</ref>).

text.text: Interpretation should, therefore, be focused primarily on expected influence and strength.
For bridge centrality, bridge strength (CS = .67) and bridge expected influence (CS = .59) showed acceptable to good stability, whereas bridge betweenness was much less stable (CS = .36; Figure S6).
text.formatted: For bridge centrality, bridge strength (CS = .67) and bridge expected influence (CS = .59) showed acceptable to good stability, whereas bridge betweenness was much less stable (CS = .36; Figure <ref type="figure">S6</ref>).

text.text: Interpretations should therefore be focused primarily on bridge strength and expected influence indices with greater caution applied to the interpretation of bridge betweenness.
The present study examined maternal depressive and anxiety symptoms, parenting, and children's social-emotional functioning as interconnected components of family emotional system.
Three findings are particularly notable.

First, maternal depression, maternal anxiety, parenting, and child social-emotional functioning formed four distinct but interconnected communities, pointing towards a well-connected yet a multidimensional family emotional system.

Second, maternal worry-related anxiety symptoms and child conduct problems were particularly influential within this structure, suggesting that persistent maternal worry and children's disruptive behaviours may be central features of this wider family emotional system.

Third, parenting characteristics emerged as important crossdomain connectors pointing towards everyday mother-child interactions as a context in which mothers' emotions and children's behaviours may influence one another.

Although our cross-sectional study cannot establish the direction of these relationships, our findings align with the argument of Wade and colleagues (2026) that children should be recognised as active participants shaping the emotional dynamics of their families, rather than passive recipients of parental influence.
text.formatted: Although our cross-sectional study cannot establish the direction of these relationships, our findings align with the argument of <ref type="bibr">Wade and colleagues (2026)</ref> that children should be recognised as active participants shaping the emotional dynamics of their families, rather than passive recipients of parental influence.

text.text: Within this system, we found that maternal worry-related anxiety symptoms were among the most influential nodes.
There may be many possible explanations for this.
For example, it could be because worry is closely connected to a broader range of emotional difficulties.

Researchers conceptualised worry as a form of repetitive negative thinking implicated across anxiety and depression (Moulds & McEvoy, 2025), and network research has identified repetitive negative thinking as a central factor between psychopathological domains (Zagaria et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Researchers conceptualised worry as a form of repetitive negative thinking implicated across anxiety and depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Moulds & McEvoy, 2025)</ref>, and network research has identified repetitive negative thinking as a central factor between psychopathological domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Zagaria et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Worry's dominance, in our network, may therefore partly reflect its shared symptom variance across maternal anxiety and depression.

It may also be that high levels of worry and anxiety occupy parents' attention during everyday exchanges with their children, linking their own emotional experiences with the interactions they share (Nicol-Harper et al., 2007; Stein et al., 2012).
text.formatted: It may also be that high levels of worry and anxiety occupy parents' attention during everyday exchanges with their children, linking their own emotional experiences with the interactions they share <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Nicol-Harper et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Stein et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: However, it is important to acknowledge that this relationship may also run in both directions, as children's behavioural difficulties could in turn be a source of worry for parents (Speyer et al., 2022), raising the possibility that parental worry may also develop in response to children's behavioural difficulties.
text.formatted: However, it is important to acknowledge that this relationship may also run in both directions, as children's behavioural difficulties could in turn be a source of worry for parents <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Speyer et al., 2022)</ref>, raising the possibility that parental worry may also develop in response to children's behavioural difficulties.

text.text: This possibility brings us to the child side of the system.
Children's conduct problems were not only the most strongly connected child domain but also a strong connecting factor across communities.

Unlike difficulties that may primarily be experienced internally (e.g., internalising difficulties), disruptive or oppositional behaviours characterised as conduct problems are expressed directly within interpersonal exchanges, hence, may be more closely linked to the wider family interactions.

Supporting this, longitudinal studies show that conduct problems may shape how parents respond to them, while parenting may also influence children's subsequent behaviours (Pardini et al., 2008; Lansford et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Supporting this, longitudinal studies show that conduct problems may shape how parents respond to them, while parenting may also influence children's subsequent behaviours <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Pardini et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Lansford et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: A large meta-analysis further supports these arguments and reports that the influence of children's conduct problems on parenting may be as strong as the influence of parenting on children's conduct problems (Pinquart, 2017).
text.formatted: A large meta-analysis further supports these arguments and reports that the influence of children's conduct problems on parenting may be as strong as the influence of parenting on children's conduct problems <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Pinquart, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: There are also significant associations between child conduct problems and parental anxiety and depression (Baker et al., 2020; Hails et al., 2018; Song et al., 2022).
text.formatted: There are also significant associations between child conduct problems and parental anxiety and depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Baker et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Hails et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Song et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Together, this supports the view that children actively shape the family emotional system, particularly through their conduct problems.

The position of parenting characteristics, as cross-domain connectors, bring these everyday mother-child interactions into a shared relational context in which mother and child emotional difficulties are intertwined.

This interpretation is consistent with the transactional theory which conceptualises development as emerging through continuing interactions between children and their environments rather than through unidirectional influences (Sameroff, 2009).
text.formatted: This interpretation is consistent with the transactional theory which conceptualises development as emerging through continuing interactions between children and their environments rather than through unidirectional influences <ref type="bibr">(Sameroff, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Parental irritability may be particularly relevant to these exchanges as research has shown a link between parental irritability and harsh parenting (Di Giunta et al. 2020; Thartori et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Parental irritability may be particularly relevant to these exchanges as research has shown a link between parental irritability and harsh parenting <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Di Giunta et al. 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Thartori et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: While parenting could represent one way through which maternal emotional experiences become relevant to children, parenting itself may also change in response to children's behaviour (Lansford et al., 2018).
text.formatted: While parenting could represent one way through which maternal emotional experiences become relevant to children, parenting itself may also change in response to children's behaviour <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Lansford et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Hence, we argue that it may be more useful to conceptualise parenting as a process connecting mothers' and children's emotions rather than simply as an intermediate step between maternal and child psychopathology.

Although parenting characteristics appeared to play an important bridging role between maternal emotional symptoms and child social-emotional functioning, the lower stability of bridge betweenness raises uncertainty about whether the current analysis reliably captures this role.
Therefore, the interpretation of parenting as a connector of the wider family emotional system should be treated with caution.
Taken together, we propose a theory of change that works with the family emotional system as a whole, rather than targeting parental anxiety, parenting, and child behaviours as separate factors.

Drawing on network theory (Borsboom, 2017), we hypothesise that supporting maternal worry and child conduct problems, within family-focused interventions, may result in greatest improvement in a shared family emotional system (i.e., mother and child).
text.formatted: Drawing on network theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Borsboom, 2017)</ref>, we hypothesise that supporting maternal worry and child conduct problems, within family-focused interventions, may result in greatest improvement in a shared family emotional system (i.e., mother and child).

text.text: Parenting characteristics may also be important intervention targets, given their role in connecting maternal emotional experiences with child social-emotional functioning.
However, the lower stability of bridge betweenness raises uncertainty about whether our analysis reliably captures this bridging role.

Our findings therefore provide a basis for future studies to examine the role of parenting in connecting maternal and child functioning and to test whether a whole-family approach leads to better outcomes than interventions targeting maternal and child difficulties separately.
Several limitations should be considered while interpreting our findings.
First, the crosssectional design precludes temporal inference, that is, our findings cannot determine the direction of effects.
Second, parenting information was available for only a small subset of the analytic sample, meaning that the role of parenting as connector nodes should be interpreted cautiously.
Finally, children's social-emotional functioning was parent-reported, introducing the possibility of reporterrelated bias.

This may be particularly important for internalising difficulties, such as emotional symptoms, which are less directly observable and for which children may provide more reliable information than their parents.
Our findings highlight the value of understanding maternal anxiety and depression, parenting, and children's social-emotional functioning together within a broader family emotional system.
We identify maternal worry and child conduct difficulties as prominent features of this system.
We propose that supporting these areas together may help interrupt patterns in which maternal and child difficulties reinforce one another.
Future longitudinal and intervention research should test whether this coordinated approach leads to shared improvements in parental wellbeing and children's socialemotional functioning.
Finally, the potential role of parenting in connecting maternal emotions and child social-emotional functioning also warrants further investigation.
